title: Mary Peltola Defeats Incumbent Republican in Alaska Senate Race
author: Callum Sutherland; Chad de Guzman
body:
Democratic challenger Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska, rounding out one of the tightest and most controversial races of the midterm elections, and marking another notable GOP loss in what is typically a reliably red state.

The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday evening, two weeks after Election Day, with Peltola securing 50.1% of the votes against Sullivan’s 45.8%. Peltola is the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Alaska since 2008. Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election.

Peltola, a Yup'ik Alaska Native, served one term in the House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025 and became the first Alaska Native member of Congress and the first woman to represent Alaska in the lower chamber. She’ll now be the first Alaska Native in the Senate.

The Alaska race is the last U.S. Senate contest to be called, partly due to the razor-thin margin between Peltola and Sullivan, but also because Alaska has a 15-day grace period after Election Day for mailed ballots to be returned to the elections office and counted. The state uses a ranked-choice voting system, which can make the process of certifying votes more complicated and would have resulted in a second round of vote tabulating if the leading candidate had received less than 50% of the first-round votes cast.

Peltola posted on social media following the election call that “there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”

Her victory puts the Senate balance of power at 56-44, in favor of Democrats, who secured control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms as the American public appeared to reject President Donald Trump amid concerns about the Iran war, inflation, and more. In the eight Senate contests that appeared least predictable, Democrats won all of them, and they even won in Mississippi too, where election forecasters had rated the race as likely Republican.

The race was dominated by controversy over allegations that independent runner Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, was a spoiler candidate, intended to confuse Alaskans and draw votes away from the incumbent Republican Senator with the same first and last name.

Despite protests from Trump, Republicans were unsuccessful in trying to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot. A federal judge on Nov. 1 dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump Administration that sought to delay certifying the results in Alaska if the incumbent Republican lost the race. "The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” ruled District Judge Sharon Gleason, referring to the Oct. 22 lawsuit.

The New York Times on Oct. 28 reported that “operatives” aligned with Peltola had “spent months recruiting candidates to peel votes from Senator Dan Sullivan.” Peltola vehemently denied the claims.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, launched a probe into the matter on Oct. 29, to investigate what he alleged to be an “organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”

On Election Day, Sen. Sullivan said “people are disgusted by what has gone down in Alaska” and alleged that America was “witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska.”

Peltola described the noise around the double Sullivan controversy as “just another distraction,” dismissing it as “stuff to sell newspapers, stuff to get subscriptions.”

Amid the fallout, Peltola’s campaign sued Alaska in an effort to obtain the records on rejected absentee ballots. The lawsuit, filed Nov. 6, argued the failure to release the records would amount to “severely prejudicing [Peltola’s] ability to monitor Alaska’s election certification process to make sure that all ballots are counted according to law.”

Alaska Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled against the campaign’s request on Nov. 11, stipulating that the records “cannot reasonably be produced at this juncture, nor redacted of confidential information.”

Trump, meanwhile, accused Peltola of “perpetrating such a terrible scheme” and argued that incumbent Sen. Sullivan should be prematurely announced as winner, even as Peltola inched slightly ahead in the counted votes. In a Truth Social post on Nov. 5, Trump said that the votes for Dan J. Sullivan, as well as those for Gerald Heikes, a GOP runner and the fourth candidate on Alaska’s ballot, should be “given to the REAL Dan Sullivan” insisting there is “no other fair solution.” Trump doubled down on his argument on Nov. 7, claiming that if all those votes were combined, then the Alaska race would be “over” and the incumbent Senator would be announced as the winner.

Aside from the controversy which dominated much of the discourse around the race, Peltola and Sullivan also clashed over proposals to build data centers in Alaska, an issue felt nationwide.

When asked about data centers, Peltola said she takes her “cue from the people of that region,” deferring to local support, provided it doesn’t strain the grid for existing ratepayers. Whereas Sullivan has pushed to bring data centers onto Alaska’s Air Force and joint military installations.

Peltola also hit out at Sullivan for continuing to support Trump’s war with Iran, which remains deeply unpopular with Americans, in part due to the financial ramifications of the conflict which has entered its ninth month. The disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route, has led to record high diesel prices.

In an NBC exit poll carried out Nov. 3, more than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities including gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.
